answer:
HYPOTHESIS (data-grounded answer to "How does incarceration affect the wealth of black individuals based on their income levels?")

Operationalization (stated explicitly): the dataset contains no income variable, so "income levels" are operationalized as baseline (1985) composite-wealth tiers (quartiles primary, tertiles robustness) among black respondents (n=3,013; 159 ever jailed 1985–1994, 2,854 not).

Hypothesis: Incarceration between 1985 and 1994 is associated with a severe, tier-dependent wealth penalty for black individuals that grows in absolute dollars with baseline wealth but is most complete — near-total wealth non-accumulation — among lower-baseline-wealth respondents. (a) In the lowest baseline tiers, jailed respondents fail to accumulate any wealth at all: median 1985→1996 wealth change is $0 for the jailed vs +$2,000 for non-jailed in the lowest quartile (Q1) and $0 vs $0 in Q2, with 71–79% of jailed respondents still at or below zero wealth in 1996 (vs 46–57% of non-jailed); by 1996 the jailed median is $0 in every tier below the top, versus $1,000–$12,000 for non-jailed peers who started in the same tier. (b) In the upper tiers, incarceration is associated with outright wealth loss: in Q3 the jailed median wealth change is −$1,400 vs +$9,400 for non-jailed (median 1996 wealth $0 vs $12,000), and in the top quartile (Q4) jailed respondents' median wealth falls from ~$15,185 to ~$9,800 (change −$8,000) while matched non-jailed peers gain (+$6,000 change; 1996 median $28,600 vs $9,800). The within-tier difference-in-differences on mean wealth change are approximately −$19K (Q1), −$16K (Q2), −$42K (Q3), and −$58K (Q4), i.e., the absolute incarceration-associated wealth gap roughly triples from the lowest to the highest baseline tier. In relative terms, jailed respondents' 1996 median wealth is essentially zero (ratio ≈ 0) in the low/middle tiers and only 0.34× their non-jailed peers even in the top quartile — so incarceration appears to prevent wealth-building entirely at low income levels and to actively erode existing wealth at higher income levels. Direction is consistent across median and mean, quartile and tertile stratification, and 1%/99% winsorization (winsorized median-change DiD: −$2,000 / $0 / −$10,800 / −$14,900 by quartile).

This is an associative hypothesis, not a causal estimate: jailed respondents were already poorer at baseline within the full sample, jailing is an inferred proxy (residence such as 'Jail'), and no causal identification is possible from these data.

payload.hypothesis: Incarceration (1985-1994, inferred proxy) is associated with a severe, baseline-tier-dependent wealth penalty for black NLSY79 respondents: at low baseline (1985) wealth tiers jailed respondents accumulate essentially no wealth by 1996 (median change $0 vs +$2,000 for non-jailed; 71-79% remain at or below zero wealth), while at higher baseline tiers they experience outright wealth loss (Q3 median change -$1,400 vs +$9,400; top-quartile -$8,000 vs +$6,000). Within-tier difference-in-differences on mean wealth change grow from about -$19K (lowest quartile) to about -$58K (highest quartile), and jailed respondents' 1996 median wealth is roughly zero relative to non-jailed peers in low/middle tiers and only 0.34x even in the top tier. Direction is robust to median vs mean, quartile vs tertile stratification, and 1%/99% winsorization. Because jailing is not random and ever_jailed is an inferred residence-based proxy, this is an associative hypothesis, not a causal estimate.
payload.workflow: 1) Loaded data/nls_incarceration_processed.csv (12,013 rows x 6 cols, no missingness); verified encodings and flagged (not dropped) extreme negatives ($-866K in 1990, $-403K in 1996, both outside the black subsample). 2) Restricted to black respondents (n=3,013; 'hipanic' treated as hispanic and excluded). 3) Operationalized 'income level' as baseline composite_wealth_1985 tiers via rank-based cuts: quartiles (primary) and tertiles (robustness). 4) Within each tier compared ever_jailed=1 vs 0 on 1985/1990/1996 composite wealth (medians primary, means secondary) and on the 1985->1996 change; headline statistic is the within-tier difference-in-differences (jailed change minus non-jailed change). 5) Secondary relative measure: jailed/non-jailed ratio of 1996 medians and of changes; share at or below zero wealth in 1996. 6) 1990 reported descriptively only (jailing year unknown). 7) Robustness: 1%/99% winsorized changes. Cell sizes: 34-45 jailed per quartile; results emphasize direction and rough magnitude, not precision.
